verdict.reasoning:
I rendered page 83 at 300 dpi and read specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines 3629-3676 (page-82/page-83 anchors at lines 3618/3650). Both source descriptions in the claim are factually accurate as far as they go, but the claim is a formatting/indentation observation dressed up as misplaced content, and its decisive assertion ('the rule hierarchy ... is unrecoverable') is false.

What the printed page actually shows (x-offsets measured on the 1546px-wide render): four distinct left margins -- '9)'/'10)' labels at x~197 (general-rule level), 'd)'..'g)' labels at x~250, '5.'/'6.' labels at x~290, and 'b.' plus 'NOTE 1' at x~335. 'NOTE 1' sits flush with the BODY text of items 5./6. (x~338) and 'NOTE 2' sits flush with the body text of 10) (x~248), so the printed nesting is exactly: 8) -> a)..g); c) -> 1...6.; 4. -> a., b.; 6. -> NOTE 1. That part of the claim is correct.

What the markdown shows: every one of those lines begins at column 0 (lines 3655, 3657, 3659, 3661, 3663, 3665, 3667, 3669, 3671, 3673, 3675). Also correct, and page-82 line 3645 does carry a 4-space indent on 'a.'. So neither source is misquoted.

Why this is not a content discrepancy:

1. NOTHING IS MISPLACED. Every sentence, every list label, and the reading order are transcribed verbatim and in the printed order. No text is missing, added, altered, or relocated to a different parent in the reading sequence. The only difference is leading whitespace. The verification standard here explicitly rejects differences that are page-break furniture, wrapping, or formatting; leading whitespace is formatting.

2. IT IS PAGE-BREAK FURNITURE, DEMONSTRABLY. The transcription resets relative indentation to column 0 at every page anchor and only re-establishes indentation for nesting that deepens WITHIN that page. Proof from the immediately preceding page: on page 81 the same GR-7 list has 'a)'/'b)' at a 3-space indent (lines 3604, 3606) and its '1.'/'2.' sub-items at 6 spaces (3612, 3614); the moment page 82 begins (line 3618) the continuation items b), c), d) of that very same list drop to column 0 (3623-3627). Page 83 starts mid-hierarchy at the third/fourth level, so its baseline is 0 and everything on it is 0. The a./b. 'sibling mismatch' the claim highlights is precisely this per-page baseline reset straddling a page boundary -- the exact class of artifact the reconciliation is instructed to disregard.

3. THE HIERARCHY IS RECOVERABLE, CONTRARY TO THE CLAIM. ISO's own label conventions encode the depth independently of indentation, and all four styles are preserved intact in the markdown: 'N)' = general rule (9), 10)), 'x)' = sub-item of a general rule (a)..g)), 'N.' = sub-item of a lettered sub-item (1...6.), 'x.' = sub-item of a numbered sub-sub-item (a., b.). d)..g) therefore cannot be read as siblings of 9)/10) -- they use a different label type, and they continue the contiguous, unbroken a),b),c),d),e),f),g) run opened under 8). Likewise 'b.' cannot be confused with the already-present 'b)', and 1.-6. read as one contiguous run under c). The claim's assertion that d)-g) 'render as siblings of general rules 9) and 10)' is simply wrong on both the label evidence and on rendering: in CommonMark 'd)' is not a list marker at all, so no renderer produces that false sibling relationship.

4. NO NORMATIVE MEANING CHANGES. NOTE 1 is non-normative and its text ('Because comments are removed during logical conversion, none are expected') is self-evidently tied to item 6 ('Comments, if any, are treated as a single space'); no implementer or extractor derives a different rule from the flat form. Nothing about REPLACE matching semantics in 7.2.4.4 GR 8 reads differently.

If the ledger wants to track transcription indentation fidelity at all, it should do so as a single document-wide cosmetic entry about the per-page indentation reset, not as a page-83 'structural / misplaced-content' finding. Rejecting.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. All text, all list labels, and the reading order on page 83 are transcribed faithfully; only leading indentation differs. The flattening is a systemic artifact of the transcription resetting indentation to column 0 at every page boundary (demonstrated by the identical reset at the page-81 -> page-82 break on lines 3604/3606 -> 3623/3627), i.e. page-break furniture. ISO's label styles -- 'N)' general rule, 'x)' sub-item, 'N.' sub-sub-item, 'x.' sub-sub-sub-item -- are all preserved and independently encode the nesting, so the 7.2.4.4 GR 8 hierarchy (8) -> a)..g); c) -> 1...6.; 4. -> a., b.; 6. -> NOTE 1) remains fully recoverable from the markdown. The claim's premises about both sources are accurate, but 'misplaced content', 'structural' severity, 'd)-g) render as siblings of 9) and 10)', and 'unrecoverable' are all overstated or incorrect. At most this is a document-wide cosmetic indentation note, not a page-83 finding.
